title: Work On or Near Water
whatItIs: There is a risk of drowning when you work beside or above water, or cross it to get to work. People can also drown in slurry lagoons, open vats and other liquids.

keyFacts.text: Steps MUST be taken to stop falls into water, minimise the risk of drowning and provide rescue equipment.
Boats taking people to or from work MUST NOT be overcrowded or overloaded.

keyFacts: Guard rails and toe boards, or a similar barrier, at open edges stop people falling in.
There should be a way to raise the alarm. Whistles and lights help find people in the water.
Life jackets should ideally be auto-inflating and always worn, by people trained to use them.
Cold water shock, waterlogged clothing, injury and hypothermia all add to the risk of drowning.

visual.caption: Four lines of defence (HSG150 paras 520-527; CDM 2015 reg 26)

items.title: Prevent the fall
items.text: Guard rails and toe boards at open edges; reduce the water flow where possible.

items.title: Raise the alarm
items.text: A way to raise the alarm; whistles and lights to locate people.

items.title: Keep afloat
items.text: Life jackets, always worn, that turn an unconscious person face up.

items.title: Rescue
items.text: Grab lines, throw lines and, where needed, a rescue boat with a competent operator.

a.label: Life jacket
points: Supports an unconscious person face up

b.label: Buoyancy aid
points: Helps a conscious person stay afloat
May not turn an unconscious person face up

onTheTest.question: Why is a life jacket chosen over a buoyancy aid for work over water?
options: It turns an unconscious person face up
It can be left off in calm water
onTheTest.why: HSG150 paras 523-524: life jackets support an unconscious person and turn them face up. A buoyancy aid may not. Wearers must be trained.

onTheTest.question: You work from a MEWP over a river, and drowning is the greater risk. What should you wear?
options: A harness clipped to the basket
A life jacket, not a harness
A harness and a hard hat
onTheTest.why: HSE GEIS6: life jackets, not harnesses, should be worn where there is a risk of drowning.

traps: Never tie a throw line to anything: in fast water a tied line can hold the person under.
A grab line goes across the river at 45° to the flow, not at 90°.
Rescue kit must be ready: the law requires that someone who falls in can be promptly rescued.
Drowning isn't only rivers and the sea: slurry lagoons and open vats count too.
